summary_paragraph: A 58-year-old woman with a history of HCV and alcoholic cirrhosis, hepatic encephalopathy, and major depression was admitted for severe right upper quadrant abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. She was found to have acute colitis likely due to infectious gastroenteritis, confirmed by CT imaging and supported by the development of loose stools during admission. Stool studies were negative for pathogens including C. difficile, Salmonella, and E. coli O157:H7. She was somnolent on admission, likely due to morphine and her acute illness, but her mental status improved with supportive care and continuation of lactulose and rifaximin. Her tachycardia was attributed to dehydration and resolved with fluids. Spironolactone was held initially due to hypovolemia but restarted before discharge. A flexible sigmoidoscopy showed hemorrhoids but no colitis or bleeding. She improved clinically, tolerated oral intake, and was discharged home with follow-up plans and instructions to avoid alcohol and marijuana.
